name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Chronological sequence of dispersion force formation

questiontext.text:
Consider the following steps involved in the development of dispersion (London) forces between two nonpolar atoms X and Y in close proximity:

  • An instantaneous dipole develops on Atom X for a very short time.
  • The temporary dipoles of Atom X and Atom Y attract each other.
  • The electronic charge distribution in Atom X momentarily becomes unsymmetrical.
  • The instantaneous dipole on Atom X distorts the electron density of Atom Y, inducing a dipole in Atom Y.

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of these events?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Atoms and nonpolar molecules are electrically symmetrical on average, so dispersion forces must originate from a spontaneous, momentary fluctuation in electron distribution.

Step 2: Chronological Evaluation
First, the electronic charge distribution in Atom X momentarily becomes unsymmetrical, with more charge cloud on one side than the other. Second, this asymmetry creates an instantaneous (transient) dipole on Atom X. Third, the instantaneous dipole distorts the electron cloud of the neighbouring Atom Y, thereby inducing a dipole in Atom Y. Finally, the temporary dipoles on Atom X and Atom Y attract each other.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct chronological sequence is: momentary unsymmetrical electron cloud in Atom X \(\rightarrow\) development of an instantaneous dipole on Atom X \(\rightarrow\) induction of a dipole in Atom Y \(\rightarrow\) attraction between the temporary dipoles of Atom X and Atom Y.

answer.text: Momentary unsymmetrical electron cloud in Atom X \(\rightarrow\) Instantaneous dipole develops on Atom X \(\rightarrow\) Dipole is induced in Atom Y \(\rightarrow\) Temporary dipoles of Atom X and Atom Y attract each other

Dipole is induced in Atom Y \(\rightarrow\) Momentary unsymmetrical electron cloud in Atom X \(\rightarrow\) Instantaneous dipole develops on Atom X \(\rightarrow\) Temporary dipoles of Atom X and Atom Y attract each other

Instantaneous dipole develops on Atom X \(\rightarrow\) Temporary dipoles of Atom X and Atom Y attract each other \(\rightarrow\) Momentary unsymmetrical electron cloud in Atom X \(\rightarrow\) Dipole is induced in Atom Y

Momentary unsymmetrical electron cloud in Atom X \(\rightarrow\) Dipole is induced in Atom Y \(\rightarrow\) Temporary dipoles of Atom X and Atom Y attract each other \(\rightarrow\) Instantaneous dipole develops on Atom X

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Increasing order of intermolecular force strength

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following attractive intermolecular interactions in increasing order of their typical strength (from weakest to strongest) for molecules of comparable size:

Dipole–dipole forces, Dispersion (London) forces, Hydrogen bonding, Dipole–induced dipole forces

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Intermolecular attractions depend on whether the interacting species possess transient dipoles, induced dipoles, permanent partial charges, or highly polar hydrogen bonds.

Step 2: Logical Ordering
Dispersion (London) forces involve only momentary transient dipoles and are generally the weakest. Dipole–induced dipole forces involve one permanent dipole inducing a dipole in a nonpolar molecule, making them stronger than pure dispersion forces for comparable sizes. Dipole–dipole forces act between two permanent dipoles and are stronger than London and dipole–induced dipole interactions. Hydrogen bonding is a particularly strong, directional case of dipole–dipole interaction involving \(\text{N–H}\), \(\text{O–H}\), or \(\text{H–F}\) bonds (\(10\text{ to }100\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)), making it the strongest among these four.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the increasing order of strength is: Dispersion (London) forces < Dipole–induced dipole forces < Dipole–dipole forces < Hydrogen bonding.

answer.text: Dipole–induced dipole forces < Dispersion (London) forces < Dipole–dipole forces < Hydrogen bonding
Dispersion (London) forces < Dipole–dipole forces < Dipole–induced dipole forces < Hydrogen bonding
Dispersion (London) forces < Dipole–induced dipole forces < Dipole–dipole forces < Hydrogen bonding
Hydrogen bonding < Dipole–dipole forces < Dipole–induced dipole forces < Dispersion (London) forces

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_SEQUENCING_Q03 - Increasing order of molecular speeds for Cl2 and N2

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following molecular speeds at \(300\text{ K}\) in increasing order (from lowest to highest):

Most probable speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\), Root mean square speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\), Most probable speed of \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\), Average speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
At the same temperature, heavier gas molecules move more slowly than lighter gas molecules, and for any single gas, the characteristic speeds follow \(u_{\text{mp}} < u_{\text{av}} < u_{\text{rms}}\) in the ratio \(1 : 1.128 : 1.224\).

Step 2: Logical Ordering
Comparing molar masses, \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) (\(71\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)) is much heavier than \(\mathrm{N_2}\) (\(28\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)), so at \(300\text{ K}\) the most probable speed of \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) is lower than the most probable speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\). For \(\mathrm{N_2}\) at \(300\text{ K}\), the most probable speed is less than the average speed, which in turn is less than the root mean square speed.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the increasing order is: Most probable speed of \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) < Most probable speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) < Average speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) < Root mean square speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\).

answer.text: Most probable speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) < Most probable speed of \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) < Average speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) < Root mean square speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\)
Most probable speed of \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) < Most probable speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) < Average speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) < Root mean square speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\)
Most probable speed of \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) < Root mean square speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) < Average speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) < Most probable speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\)
Average speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) < Most probable speed of \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) < Most probable speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) < Root mean square speed of \(\mathrm{N_2}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_SEQUENCING_Q04 - Chronological order of liquefaction on cooling from 500 K

questiontext.text: The critical temperatures (\(T_c\)) of four gases are: \(\mathrm{NH_3} = 405.5\text{ K}\), \(\mathrm{CO_2} = 304.10\text{ K}\), \(\mathrm{O_2} = 154.3\text{ K}\), and \(\mathrm{H_2} = 33.2\text{ K}\). If separate samples of these gases at \(500\text{ K}\) are cooled gradually under sufficient pressure, in what chronological order will they reach their critical temperatures and begin to liquefy (from first to last)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A gas can only be liquefied by compression once its temperature is at or below its critical temperature \(T_c\). When cooling from a high temperature such as \(500\text{ K}\), the gas with the highest \(T_c\) reaches its liquefaction threshold first.

Step 2: Chronological Evaluation
As temperature drops from \(500\text{ K}\), \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) reaches \(405.5\text{ K}\) first. Next, \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) reaches \(304.10\text{ K}\). Upon further cooling, \(\mathrm{O_2}\) reaches \(154.3\text{ K}\), and finally \(\mathrm{H_2}\) requires cooling all the way down to \(33.2\text{ K}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the chronological order of liquefaction from first to last is: \(\mathrm{NH_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_2}\).

answer.text: \(\mathrm{H_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH_3}\)
\(\mathrm{CO_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_2}\)
\(\mathrm{NH_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_2}\)
\(\mathrm{NH_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_2}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_SEQUENCING_Q05 - Increasing order of normal boiling points of liquids

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following liquids in increasing order of their normal boiling points (from lowest to highest):

Water, Diethyl ether, Ethyl alcohol, Carbon tetrachloride

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The normal boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid's vapour pressure reaches \(760\text{ mm Hg}\) (\(1\text{ atm}\)). Liquids with higher vapour pressure at a given temperature have weaker intermolecular forces and lower normal boiling points.

Step 2: Logical Ordering
From the vapour pressure–temperature curves of these liquids, diethyl ether boils at \(308\text{ K}\), carbon tetrachloride at \(349.7\text{ K}\), ethyl alcohol at \(351.3\text{ K}\), and water at \(373\text{ K}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the increasing order of normal boiling points is: Diethyl ether < Carbon tetrachloride < Ethyl alcohol < Water.

answer.text: Diethyl ether < Carbon tetrachloride < Ethyl alcohol < Water
Diethyl ether < Ethyl alcohol < Carbon tetrachloride < Water
Carbon tetrachloride < Diethyl ether < Ethyl alcohol < Water
Water < Ethyl alcohol < Carbon tetrachloride < Diethyl ether

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_SEQUENCING_Q06 - Stages of isothermal compression of CO2 below Tc

questiontext.text:
When gaseous carbon dioxide at \(21.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) (below its critical temperature \(30.98\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)) is compressed isothermally from low pressure to very high pressure, the following stages occur:

  • Liquid and gaseous \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) coexist in equilibrium at constant pressure as more gas condenses.
  • Only gaseous \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is present, and its pressure rises as volume decreases.
  • All gas has condensed, and further compression causes a steep rise in pressure with very little decrease in volume.
  • Liquid \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) of a particular volume appears for the first time at the boundary of the two-phase region.

Which option gives the correct chronological order of these stages during compression?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
On Andrews' \(p\)–\(V\) isotherm below the critical temperature (\(21.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C} < 30.98\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)), compression proceeds from the gas region, across the two-phase dome, into the liquid region.

Step 2: Chronological Evaluation
Initially, at large volume and low pressure, only gaseous \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) exists and pressure rises as volume decreases. Upon reaching the right boundary of the dome, liquid \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) appears for the first time. Further reduction in volume keeps the pressure constant while liquid and gas coexist in equilibrium and gas condenses into liquid. Once the left boundary of the dome is reached, all gas has condensed into liquid, and any further compression produces a steep rise in pressure because liquids have very low compressibility.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the correct chronological sequence is: Only gas present with rising pressure \(\rightarrow\) First appearance of liquid \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) \(\rightarrow\) Coexistence of liquid and gas at constant pressure \(\rightarrow\) Complete condensation followed by steep pressure rise on compressing the liquid.

answer.text: First appearance of liquid \(\rightarrow\) Only gas present \(\rightarrow\) Coexistence at constant pressure \(\rightarrow\) Steep pressure rise of compressed liquid
Only gas present \(\rightarrow\) Coexistence at constant pressure \(\rightarrow\) First appearance of liquid \(\rightarrow\) Steep pressure rise of compressed liquid
Only gas present \(\rightarrow\) First appearance of liquid \(\rightarrow\) Coexistence at constant pressure \(\rightarrow\) Steep pressure rise of compressed liquid
Steep pressure rise of compressed liquid \(\rightarrow\) Coexistence at constant pressure \(\rightarrow\) First appearance of liquid \(\rightarrow\) Only gas present

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_STATES_OF_MATTER_SEQUENCING_Q07 - Continuous single-phase path from gas to liquid CO2

questiontext.text: To demonstrate the continuity of the gaseous and liquid states, gaseous \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) at \(21.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) can be converted into liquid \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) at \(21.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) while keeping the substance in a single phase throughout (never entering the two-phase dome). Which chronological sequence of steps accomplishes this transformation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
To bypass the two-phase dome on a \(p\)–\(V\) diagram, the path must go around the critical point (\(T_c = 30.98\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)) by first moving above \(T_c\), then compressing to a liquid-like volume, and finally cooling back below \(T_c\).

Step 2: Chronological Evaluation
First, heat the gas at constant volume from \(21.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to above the critical temperature (e.g., \(31.1\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)). Second, compress the fluid isothermally along the \(31.1\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) isotherm to a high pressure and small volume (to the left of \(V_c\)). Third, cool the compressed fluid at constant volume, crossing the critical isotherm into the liquid region without passing through the two-phase dome, until reaching liquid \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) at \(21.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the correct sequence is: Heat at constant volume above \(T_c\) \(\rightarrow\) Compress isothermally above \(T_c\) to small volume \(\rightarrow\) Cool at constant volume across the critical isotherm to obtain liquid \(\mathrm{CO_2}\).

answer.text: Compress isothermally at \(21.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to small volume \(\rightarrow\) Heat at constant volume above \(T_c\) \(\rightarrow\) Cool at constant volume back to \(21.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)

Heat at constant volume above \(T_c\) \(\rightarrow\) Compress isothermally above \(T_c\) to small volume \(\rightarrow\) Cool at constant volume across the critical isotherm to \(21.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)
Cool at constant volume below \(21.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) \(\rightarrow\) Compress isothermally to small volume \(\rightarrow\) Heat at constant volume above \(T_c\)
Compress isothermally above \(T_c\) \(\rightarrow\) Heat at constant volume above \(T_c\) \(\rightarrow\) Expand isothermally into the two-phase dome
